title: A Multi-Platform Learning Management System for Institute of Computing Studies at Colegio de Montalban
conceptual: The conceptual framework follows the Input–Process–Output (IPO) model with feedback, as shown in Figure 1. It organizes the study’s requirements and resources, development and evaluation activities, and expected system output. Purwanto et al. (2025) examined limitations of linear IPO representations and proposed an IMOI adaptation in which outputs and feedback inform subsequent iterations. The present study retains IPO while incorporating feedback into requirement refinement and succeeding development cycles.

The Input component comprises related literature, initial academic practices and concerns within ICS, and system requirements. The literature covers academic management, programming coursework, learning support, and collaboration. Local requirements gathering will examine the use of separate academic and productivity tools, resource management, faculty coordination, and access conditions. These concerns will be investigated rather than reported as established local findings in advance.

Technical inputs include development workstations, supported client devices, Next.js services, PostgreSQL, web browsers, the Expo mobile application, and the Electron Administrator Console. Connectivity, persistent storage, programming execution, repository access, authorization, continuity arrangements, and test configurations will define the operating environment. Estimated equipment specifications will be distinguished from configurations demonstrated during evaluation.

The Process component combines iterative development with requirements-based testing and software-quality evaluation. Planning, Design, Development, Testing, Deployment, and Review will organize successive increments. The modules will address academic management, computing coursework, personal study, gamification, collaboration, academic coordination, and administration. Their availability will follow Student, Instructor, Super User, and Administrator permissions and the complementary responsibilities of the three applications.

The evaluation will use six selected ISO/IEC 25010:2023 characteristics: Functional Suitability, Interaction Capability, Security, Performance Efficiency, Reliability, and Compatibility (ISO, 2023). Respondent ratings will describe experiences with assigned tasks, while technical checks will examine calculations, access restrictions, record handling, performance, and shared information. Abid et al. (2024) provides a feature-based example of systematic LMS evaluation; the study’s quality characteristics are derived from ISO/IEC 25010:2023.

The Output is the developed and evaluated CdM LMS release for ICS. It will provide a principal Web Portal, selected mobile support, and a native Administrator Console around shared records and authorized workflows. Feedback from testing, evaluation, and review will return to the Input component to refine requirements and priorities. Revised inputs will guide subsequent development cycles. Findings will concern the evaluated release and will not establish long-term educational effects or institution-wide adoption.
operational: The researchers will use an adapted Agile development approach consisting of Planning, Design, Development, Testing, Deployment, and Review. Alsaqqa et al. (2020) describes Agile values, iterative methods, and responsiveness to changing requirements. The six stages used here are the project’s operational organization rather than a universal Agile sequence. Each cycle will address prioritized requirements and produce an increment for examination and refinement.

Planning Phase. The researchers will gather local requirements from ICS students, instructors, and relevant academic and administrative personnel. Llamas et al. (2025) identifies LMS usability and workflow concerns, while Guico (2026) highlights preparation, resource access, and training needs. These findings inform topics for local investigation. Requirements will specify role responsibilities, platform coverage, expected behavior, and acceptance criteria in a prioritized backlog.

Design Phase. Architecture, database relationships, workflows, and interfaces will be prepared from the requirements. Flowcharts, ERDs, and DFDs will identify information movement and component responsibilities. Attention to navigation and task feedback is supported by the user-experience concerns examined by Laspiñas and Almerez (2024). The design will separate academic supervision from teaching and administration and protect personal academic records.

Development Phase. Selected functions will be implemented incrementally using the Next.js backend, PostgreSQL database, and applicable clients. Development will connect academic management, programming coursework, study tools, gamification, collaboration, coordination, and administration. Each increment will be checked against its acceptance criteria. The release record will distinguish implemented, proposed, tested, and evaluation-enabled functions.

Testing Phase. Controlled accounts and datasets will be used to examine correctness, authorization, integrity, integration, performance, and failure handling. The evaluation release will also undergo role-appropriate task assessment aligned with the six selected ISO/IEC 25010:2023 characteristics (ISO, 2023). Technical results and respondent ratings will be reported separately. Defects will be corrected and retested before affected functions are evaluated.

Deployment Phase. A reviewed release will be configured in a controlled environment. The researchers will verify startup, backend connectivity, accounts, client builds, and available continuity procedures. Participants will receive task guidance. The release version, enabled modules, device configurations, and unresolved limitations will be recorded; controlled evaluation will not be described as institution-wide deployment.

Review Phase. The researchers will examine technical observations, questionnaire responses, and task feedback from eligible ICS users and qualified IT experts. Findings will identify supported behavior, defects, and refinement priorities. These priorities will return to the backlog for the next cycle, and corrected functions will undergo further testing.
scope: The study covers the development and software-quality evaluation of CdM LMS for the Institute of Computing Studies at Colegio de Montalban, including BSIT and BSCpE students, instructors, and supporting academic and administrative workflows. Participation is not restricted to one student year level. IBE and ITE configuration is a technical application capability; those institutes are outside the research population and generalization of findings.

The Web Portal is the principal academic environment and the initial platform for the coordination expansion. Mobile provides selected academic and productivity functions according to the evaluated build. The native Desktop Application is the Administrator Console. Super User oversight is web-based; native mobile parity for the expansion and native Super User console entry are excluded. A role and platform matrix will identify the functions actually tested.

Functional coverage includes course resources and submissions, the Dynamic Gradebook, descriptive analytics, separate CodeLab and Git coursework workflows, Knowledge Exchange, personal notes and study tools, gamified progression, faculty organization, restricted supervision, schedules, targeted events, and administration. Dean and Program Head are academic designations attached to eligible accounts. They do not replace the four primary roles or automatically grant Super User privileges.

Evaluation will use criterion-based purposive sampling of eligible ICS students and instructors with prior LMS experience and qualified IT experts. Participants must voluntarily agree and perform relevant tasks before rating them. Full eligibility, recruitment, task assignment, and sample justification procedures are specified in Chapter 3. Validator participation is separate from respondent participation.

Operation depends on supported devices, connectivity, and service availability. The study does not claim universal operating-system support, identical platform functions, uninterrupted service, or full offline coursework. Hardware figures are estimates until tested. Programming languages, repository access, reporting, and continuity coverage will be limited to the documented evaluation release.

Academic analytics describe existing records. Rule-based attention indicators do not predict future achievement. CodeLab checks predefined cases, while Git history supports review without proving authorship or eliminating plagiarism. Tab switching, copy/paste, and fullscreen events are contextual assessment indicators rather than conclusive cheating evidence. Optional grade incentives will be evaluated only when their effect and institutional authorization are documented; EXP, forum reputation, and academic grades remain distinct measures.

Scheduling uses Asia/Manila, selected weekdays, one shared time pair, date bounds, and effective-dated revisions. Individual future classes may be cancelled, rescheduled, or restored. Arbitrary recurrence, multiple weekly time patterns, automatic attendance, holiday cancellation, room-conflict prevention, and timetable optimization are excluded. Student recurring timetable projection is excluded; authorized events and coursework deadlines remain available.

Supervision excludes student identities, individual grades, submissions, attempts, answers, and teaching controls. Event audiences govern LMS visibility without implying external delivery or Google synchronization. Note–event conversion creates private snapshots; later edits do not propagate. The descriptive study will not determine long-term changes in achievement, motivation, employability, or study habits. Findings apply to the selected ICS participants, tasks, and evaluated release.
features: Authorized instructors organize courses, sections, learning materials, annotations, assignments, announcements, and deadlines. Students request enrollment using valid join codes and obtain course-workspace access after approval. Streams, classwork, people, and grades present information according to enrollment and course permissions.

The Dynamic Gradebook uses configured assessment components, weights, and recorded scores to compute grades. Students view their own grade information; instructors review authorized class summaries and export permitted CSV records. Rule-based attention indicators use available activity and performance records. Computation and chart outputs will be verified against controlled data.

CodeLab provides browser-based code writing, execution, and submission assessed against instructor-defined test cases. Git-integrated coursework separately connects authorized repository submissions to instructor review. Repository authorization remains separate from LMS authentication. Execution languages, service configuration, and supported submission paths will be recorded for the evaluation release.

Owned notes, personal tasks, authorized calendar items, flashcards, review/mastery records, focus timers, and study-session tracking support organization and repeated study. Users may schedule an owned note as a private event or save a readable persisted event as a private note. Conversion reuses linked results and creates snapshots rather than continuous synchronization.

Configured participation earns EXP, levels, achievements, badges, streaks, and permitted rankings. Knowledge Exchange supports academic questions, answers, and resource sharing, with instructor moderation and Faculty-Verified Answers. Forum reputation is separate from EXP and grades. Reward or incentive rules will be documented and evaluated only within their approved scope.

The ICS directory and organizational chart identify the Dean, BSIT and BSCpE Program Heads, and faculty memberships. General means neither track; Cross-program means both. Course program classification remains independent of faculty membership. Super Users use the web academic hub to inspect authorized summaries, faculty information, timetables, and restricted course supervision, and make narrowly permitted leadership assignments.

Authorized instructors and Administrators manage date-bounded weekly schedules and occurrence exceptions. Effective revisions preserve earlier times, rooms, and instructor attribution. Day, Week, Month, and Year views distinguish saved events, projected classes, and syllabus deadlines; Year uses density summaries. Explicit audiences include Personal, Course, Institute Faculty, BSIT Instructors, and BSCpE Instructors. Program Heads may publish to the documented ICS audiences without gaining ownership of other creators’ content.

The native Administrator Console provides account status and role operations, instructor assignments, configuration, logs, and supported reporting and continuity functions. Only Administrators provision or revoke Super User accounts. The backend checks sessions and applicable role, institute, ownership, enrollment, and resource relationships. Protected operations use validation, audit records, and the transactions or version checks specified by the feature contract.

The clients retrieve applicable shared information through authorized Next.js workflows. Updates become available according to implemented retrieval or synchronization behavior and connectivity. In-LMS notifications and the platform help chatbot support navigation and academic tasks. Feature presence does not establish universal native parity, external notification delivery, or an AI tutoring function.
design: The study will combine iterative system development, requirements-based technical verification, and quantitative descriptive evaluation. Descriptive research systematically characterizes observed conditions and experiences without establishing causal effects (McCombes, 2023). Questionnaires will describe users’ experiences with assigned tasks; controlled technical checks will examine correctness, access restrictions, record handling, performance, and integration. The two evidence types will be reported separately and considered together.

The Agile operational framework in Section 1.5 will guide development. Chapter 3 specifies how local requirements, evaluation participants, instruments, tests, and analysis will be organized. The evaluation will address six selected ISO/IEC 25010:2023 characteristics rather than claim assessment of the complete standard or ISO certification.
overview: CdM LMS connects the principal Web Portal, complementary Expo/React Native application, and native Electron Administrator Console to Next.js backend workflows and PostgreSQL records. Students access approved coursework and their own academic and study information. Instructors manage assigned teaching activities. Super Users perform restricted academic coordination through the web; Administrators operate the native console. Program Head and Dean designations remain separate from those account roles.

The evaluation configuration will identify enabled modules, client builds, roles, and datasets. Existing functions and proposed coordination extensions will have separate implementation and test-status entries. Only demonstrated functions will be included in respondent tasks and reported as evaluated.
requirements: Before finalizing the development backlog, the researchers will seek institutional permission to gather local requirements from relevant ICS students, instructors, and designated academic or administrative personnel. Planned methods include guided interviews or small-group consultations and examination of available workflow descriptions. Topics will cover resource distribution, enrollment, submissions, grading, programming coursework, personal organization, faculty coordination, and device/network access.

With consent, the researchers will record de-identified notes, summarize recurring needs, and validate the resulting requirement statements with appropriate stakeholders. Each accepted requirement will identify its user, applicable platform, expected behavior, access restrictions, and acceptance criteria. These pre-development consultations are distinct from the post-development software-quality questionnaires.
respondents: Respondents will comprise selected ICS students, ICS instructors, and qualified IT experts. Students must be officially enrolled in BSIT or BSCpE, have prior LMS experience, understand common academic tasks, and voluntarily perform the evaluation activities. Instructors must teach within ICS, have relevant LMS experience, and voluntarily complete their assigned teaching or coordination tasks. IT experts must have relevant qualifications, training, or experience in software development, testing, database management, cybersecurity, or system administration.

Students will evaluate enrolled coursework, submissions, personal grades, study tools, and collaboration that they have used. Instructors will evaluate assigned course management, assessment, grading, enrollment, and communication. Program Heads may evaluate designation-specific event publication. A Program Head designation will not be used as evidence of Super User authorization. Qualified experts may use controlled Super User and Administrator accounts to inspect oversight and console functions without unrestricted access to real student records.

The adviser and three proposed faculty validators will review instrument content separately from the evaluation sample. They will become respondents only if they independently meet the selection criteria. Target numbers for each respondent group will be justified after confirming eligible participants and feasible task sessions; the final report will identify invited, participating, and valid responding counts separately.
sampling: Criterion-based purposive sampling will select participants whose experience and role allow them to evaluate the relevant functions. Memon et al. (2025) emphasizes explicit and justified selection criteria in quantitative purposive sampling. Institutional enrollment alone will not qualify a participant to rate every platform or administrative function.

Following institutional permission, eligible participants will be invited through an approved recruitment process. The invitation will describe the study, tasks, participation conditions, and voluntary nature of involvement. The researchers will screen role and experience criteria, arrange task sessions, and record participation and nonresponse by group. Sample justification will reflect coverage of roles, functions, and feasible evaluation conditions; findings will not be represented as probability estimates for the entire ICS population.
instruments: Two questionnaire sets will be prepared: a user instrument with Student and Instructor sections, and an IT-expert instrument for relevant technical, supervision, and administrative functions. Both will align with the selected quality characteristics. Items will describe one observable behavior and identify the task or function needed to answer them. Respondents will rate only the functions they have directly used.

Responses will use Strongly Agree (4), Agree (3), Disagree (2), and Strongly Disagree (1). A separate Not applicable or not observed option will receive no numeric score. The adviser and proposed validators will review clarity, relevance, role suitability, and alignment. A pilot with eligible participants outside the main sample will examine instructions and item interpretation. Content review and internal-consistency analysis of actual pilot responses will be distinguished; reviewer approval alone will not establish reliability.

Participants will receive orientation and consent information, use assigned test accounts where applicable, and perform a documented task sequence before completing the questionnaire. The researchers will record role, platform/build, task completion, and encountered issues. Technical checks will use a separate record of setup, expected and actual results, errors, measurements, and retest outcomes.
analysis: Questionnaire responses will be tabulated by respondent group, item, and quality characteristic. Frequencies and percentages will describe response distributions. The valid count for each item will exclude unanswered and Not applicable or not observed responses; those exclusions will also be reported. N/A will not be treated as zero, disagreement, or a passing result.

For comparability with the coded scale, an item mean will be calculated as the sum of valid response scores divided by the valid response count. Equivalently, the frequency-weighted mean is (4f4 + 3f3 + 2f2 + f1) / (f4 + f3 + f2 + f1). Frequency weighting represents counts of responses, not different importance weights for users or quality characteristics. Response distributions and valid counts will accompany means; median summaries may be reported to retain visibility of the ordered categories.

Characteristic summaries will first be computed for each respondent from the applicable items, then summarized within the Student, Instructor, or expert group. The number of applicable items and contributing respondents will be reported. Results from different roles or questionnaire versions will not be pooled into one score unless item equivalence and weighting are explicitly justified. Numeric results will be reported on the 1–4 scale without unapproved labels such as highly acceptable.

Technical results will be reported by test case and characteristic. Correctness and access cases will identify expected/actual outcomes and pass, fail, or not executed status. Timings will identify workload, repetitions, median and observed slow cases; resource observations will identify the measurement conditions. Favorable questionnaire means will not override failed authorization, calculation, or persistence tests. The study will use descriptive summaries and will not claim causal educational effects or population-wide statistical representation.
ethics: The researchers will obtain applicable institutional permission before recruitment or access to restricted records. Participants will receive information about purpose, tasks, duration, data use, and voluntary participation. Declining or withdrawing will not affect grades, employment, or access to ordinary institutional services. Consent will be obtained before task participation and questionnaire collection.

Evaluation identifiers will replace participant names in analysis files. The researchers will use controlled accounts and synthetic or appropriately de-identified academic records for restricted tests. Only authorized members of the research team and approved reviewers will access identifiable materials. Storage location, access controls, retention period, and deletion arrangements will be specified in the approved protocol. Public reports will present aggregate results and avoid exposing credentials, repository tokens, or personal academic records.
testing: A test matrix will map requirements to selected quality characteristics, account roles, platforms, datasets, and expected outcomes. Each case will record the application revision, enabled feature, setup, action, result, error evidence, and retest status. Calculation checks will compare outputs with manually verified expected records. Security cases will invoke prohibited reads/writes directly rather than rely on hidden interface buttons.

The researchers will define workload and dataset sizes before performance testing. Logged-in sessions, request rates, simultaneous programming executions, and upload sizes will be recorded separately; a registered-account count will not establish concurrent capacity. Repeated timing checks will distinguish ordinary retrieval, grade computation, calendar queries, file transfer, and CodeLab execution. Thresholds will be approved and recorded before judging performance.

Reliability checks will examine saved records after refresh, interrupted requests, retries, duplicate conversion, stale saves, and relevant concurrent updates. Compatibility checks will verify shared records through permitted clients and observe the Administrator Console alongside selected workstation software. Migration and restoration rehearsals will use an isolated database. Unexecuted or failed cases will remain visible in the evaluation record; fresh evidence will support any reported pass.
